lead: This unit explains how bits become reliable frames and share a common medium. After studying, you can build and analyse data‑link protocols such as Ethernet, HDLC or Wi‑Fi.
about: Unit 3 covers nine topics. Chapter 3.1 introduces framing and bit stuffing. Chapter 3.2 adds error detection using parity, checksum and CRC. Chapter 3.3 shows single‑error correction with Hamming codes. Chapter 3.4 explains flow control with stop‑and‑wait and sliding‑window. Chapter 3.5 adds ARQ mechanisms Go‑Back‑N and Selective Repeat. Chapter 3.6 describes HDLC and PPP framing. Chapter 3.7 compares multiple‑access schemes ALOHA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA. Chapter 3.8 details Ethernet frames and VLAN tagging. Chapter 3.9 finishes with IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN architecture and MAC.

chapters.idea: Convert a bit stream into frames and delimit them with bit stuffing.
chapters.depth: Explain start/stop flag 01111110, bit‑stuff rule (insert 0 after five consecutive 1s), and why framing is needed for a continuous physical channel. Mention alternate name byte stuffing. Show how receiver removes stuffed bits.

figure.aria: Shows how bits are stuffed, framed, sent, then destuffed.

chapters.example: Data bits = 1101111110. After stuffing: 11011111010 (a 0 inserted after five 1s). Add flag 01111110 at both ends → 01111110 11011111010 01111110.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to remove the inserted 0 gives a wrong payload length.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 basics of bits and bytes.
chapters.leave: Physical‑layer line coding and modulation are covered in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Detect corrupted frames using parity, checksum and CRC.
chapters.depth: Define even and odd parity bit, 2‑D parity (row and column), 16‑bit checksum as one's‑complement sum of words, and CRC with generator polynomial G(x)=x³+x+1. Explain why each method catches certain error patterns.

figure.title: Parity and checksum table
figure.aria: Shows data words, checksum column and parity row.

chapters.example: Words: 0xABCD, 0x1234, 0xFFFF. Sum = 0xABCD+0x1234+0xFFFF = 0x1C9A6. Mod 2¹⁶ gives 0x9A6. One's complement checksum = 0xF659.
chapters.trap: Using ordinary addition instead of one's‑complement for the checksum leads to a wrong result.
chapters.leave: Error‑correction codes are treated in Chapter 3.

chapters.idea: Correct a single‑bit error by adding Hamming parity bits.
chapters.depth: Describe (7,4) Hamming code: parity bits at positions 1,2,4; data bits at 3,5,6,7. Show syndrome calculation as XOR of received parity checks. Mention extended (8,4) SEC‑DED as an advanced topic taught by only a few universities.

figure.title: (7,4) Hamming positions
figure.aria: Shows which bit positions hold parity (p) and data (d).

chapters.example: Data = 1011. Parity bits: p1=0, p2=1, p3=0. Encoded word = 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 (0110011). Flip bit 3 → 0 1 0 0 0 1 1. Syndrome = 3 → correct bit 3 back to 1.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the order of syndrome bits gives the wrong error location.
chapters.leave: Flow‑control and ARQ are covered in Chapters 4 and 5.

chapters.idea: Prevent sender overflow with stop‑and‑wait or sliding‑window flow control.
chapters.depth: Define sender window, acknowledgement, timeout, and efficiency η = 1/(1+2a) where a = propagation delay / transmission time. For sliding window, show window size N and cumulative ACK. Mention that Go‑Back‑N is an ARQ variant discussed later.

figure.aria: Shows stop‑and‑wait exchange of a data frame and its acknowledgement.

chapters.example: Link rate = 1 Mbps, frame = 1000 bits, one‑way delay = 20 ms. Transmission time = 1 ms, a = 20 ms/1 ms = 20. Efficiency = 1/(1+2×20)=1/41≈2.4 %.
chapters.trap: Ignoring the return propagation delay makes a too small, inflating efficiency.
chapters.leave: ARQ mechanisms are detailed in Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: Retransmit lost or corrupted frames using Go‑Back‑N or Selective Repeat.
chapters.depth: Explain sender and receiver windows, cumulative ACK for Go‑Back‑N, selective ACK for Selective Repeat, sequence numbers modulo, and required buffer sizes. Define ARQ = Automatic Repeat reQuest.

figure.aria: Shows sender window, timer expiry and retransmission in Go‑Back‑N.

chapters.example: Window size = 4. Sender transmits frames 0‑3. Frame 2 lost. Go‑Back‑N: sender retransmits 2,3 after timeout. Selective Repeat: only frame 2 is retransmitted; frame 3 is kept in buffer.
chapters.trap: Using the same window size for both protocols without extra buffer causes overflow in Selective Repeat.
chapters.leave: Specific bit‑oriented protocols HDLC and PPP are covered in Chapter 6.

chapters.idea: Provide reliable point‑to‑point links with HDLC and PPP framing.
chapters.depth: Describe HDLC flag 01111110, address, control, data, FCS (CRC‑16). List three modes: Normal Response, Asynchronous Balanced, Extended. Explain PPP encapsulation, LCP negotiation, protocol field, and reuse of HDLC‑style framing. Mention ISO‑3309 as another name.

figure.aria: Shows HDLC frame fields in order, returning to flag.

chapters.example: Data = 0xAB. HDLC frame: Flag 0x7E, Address 0xFF, Control 0x03, Data 0xAB, FCS (CRC‑16) = 0x1D0F. Bit sequence = 01111110 11111111 00000011 10101011 0001110100001111 01111110.
chapters.trap: Applying bit stuffing after adding the FCS leads to missed flag detection.
chapters.leave: Multiple‑access protocols are introduced in Chapter 7.

chapters.idea: Share a common channel using ALOHA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA.
chapters.depth: Explain pure ALOHA (throughput S = G·e^(−2G)), slotted ALOHA (S = G·e^(−G)), where G is offered load. Describe CSMA/CD operation, collision detection, exponential backoff, Ethernet slot time = 512 bits. Describe CSMA/CA for Wi‑Fi, RTS/CTS handshake, and backoff slots of 20 µs.

figure.aria: Shows theoretical throughput curves for pure and slotted ALOHA.

chapters.example: Ten stations each generate 0.02 frames per packet time. Offered load G = 10×0.02 = 0.2. Slotted ALOHA throughput S = 0.2·e^(−0.2) ≈ 0.163 frames per slot.
chapters.trap: Using the pure ALOHA formula for a slotted system overestimates throughput.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 framing and Chapter 4 flow control.
chapters.leave: Ethernet specifics and VLANs are covered in Chapter 8.

chapters.idea: Transmit Ethernet frames and separate traffic with VLAN tags.
chapters.depth: Detail Ethernet II frame: 48‑bit destination and source MAC, 16‑bit EtherType, payload (46‑1500 bytes), CRC‑32 FCS. Explain 802.1Q VLAN tag: 4‑byte field, 12‑bit VLAN ID, 3‑bit priority. Mention minimum frame size 64 bytes and its relevance to collision detection.

figure.aria: Shows Ethernet II frame with 802.1Q VLAN tag inserted.

chapters.example: Payload = 1500 bytes, header = 14 bytes, VLAN tag = 4 bytes, FCS = 4 bytes. Total bits = (1500+14+4+4)×8 = 12176 bits. On a 100 Mbps link, transmission time = 12176 bits ÷ 100 Mbps = 121.76 µs.
chapters.trap: Ignoring the 64‑byte minimum frame size leads to an invalid Ethernet frame.
chapters.leave: Wireless LAN details are in Chapter 9.

chapters.idea: Provide CSMA/CA MAC for Wi‑Fi using RTS/CTS and acknowledgements.
chapters.depth: Describe BSS, SSID, AP, stations. List frame types: management, control, data. Explain DCF operation, backoff slots of 20 µs, RTS/CTS handshake, ACK timeout, and optional advanced topics like 802.11ac MU‑MIMO (only a few universities teach it).

figure.aria: Shows CSMA/CA RTS/CTS handshake and data exchange.

chapters.example: Backoff window CW = 15. Random integer k = 7. Backoff time = k × 20 µs = 140 µs before sending RTS.
chapters.trap: Using the 9 µs slot time of 2.4 GHz for a 5 GHz network gives an incorrect backoff calculation.
chapters.leave: Transport‑layer protocols are covered in Unit 5.

links: bit stuffing prepares frames for error detection
error detection leads to correction techniques
corrected bits are used by flow control
HDLC framing similar to Ethernet framing
VLAN concepts extend to wireless LANs
